title: Design Search Autocomplete (Trie + Top-K)
prompt: Design an autocomplete system. You're given historical sentences and their usage counts. Implement input(c): the user types characters one at a time; each call returns the top 3 historical sentences that start with the prefix typed so far, ordered by descending frequency, ties broken by ASCII (lexicographic) order. A special character '#' ends the current sentence, saving it (or incrementing its count) and resetting the prefix. Return fewer than 3 if fewer match.
blurb: A trie over sentences with frequency-aware top-k retrieval per prefix — plus how you'd scale the ranking beyond a single machine.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Grasps the streaming input(c) contract, the '#' save-and-reset semantics, and the exact ranking rule (freq desc, then lexicographic).

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Chooses a trie keyed by characters with frequency stored at sentence-terminal nodes; retrieves candidates under the current prefix and selects top-3.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Maintains the growing prefix across input calls; on '#' inserts/increments and resets; correct tie-break (higher freq first, then smaller string); once a prefix has no matches, all further chars in that sentence also have none.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: Insert O(L); per-keystroke retrieval O(p + m log 3) where p=prefix len, m=matches under prefix; discusses the cost of collecting all matches vs caching top-k at nodes.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean TrieNode (children map, sentence->count at terminals or a counts map), a prefix pointer advanced per keystroke, a heap/partial-sort for top-k.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Prefix with no matches (return []), fewer than 3 matches, duplicate sentence (increment), ties resolved lexicographically, empty/reset after '#', spaces as valid characters.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Drives a full type-then-'#' cycle and verifies ranking, tie-breaks, and that a new sentence becomes searchable next time.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: States the ranking contract and the trie design before coding, and reasons about the retrieval-vs-precompute tradeoff.

constraints: Sentences consist of lowercase letters and spaces (space is a real character, part of the key)
'#' terminates a sentence: save it or increment its count, then reset the current prefix
Return top 3 by frequency descending; break ties by ASCII/lexicographic ascending
Up to ~10^5 sentences, sentence length up to ~100; many input(c) calls

examples.input: init: ["i love you":5, "island":3, "iroman":2, "i love leetcode":2]. Then input('i'), input(' '), input('a'), input('#')
examples.output: ['i love you','island','i love leetcode']; then ['i love you','i love leetcode']; then []; then []
examples.explanation: After 'i': all four start with 'i'; top 3 by freq are i love you(5), island(3), then i love leetcode and iroman tie at 2 -> lexicographic 'i love leetcode' < 'iroman', so it wins the 3rd slot. After 'i ': only the two 'i love...' match. After 'i a': nothing matches, return []. '#' saves 'i a' (count 1) and resets.

test_cases.expected: ['i love you','island','i love leetcode'] — tie at freq 2 broken lexicographically

test_cases.input: type a prefix matching nothing, e.g. input('z')
test_cases.expected: [] — and every subsequent char before '#' also returns []

test_cases.input: type an existing sentence fully then '#', then type it again
test_cases.expected: its count increments; it ranks higher on the next round

test_cases.input: two sentences same freq and one is a prefix of the other

reference.optimal_time: input(c): O(p + m log k) where p = current prefix length, m = matches under the prefix, k = 3; insert on '#': O(L). With top-k cached at nodes: O(1) amortized per keystroke.
reference.optimal_space: O(total characters across all sentences) for the trie; O(distinct sentences) for the counts

approaches.name: brute force (scan all sentences per keystroke)
approaches.idea: Keep a hashmap sentence->count. On each input(c) build the prefix and linearly scan every stored sentence for those starting with it, then sort/partial-sort for top 3. Simple but O(total data) per keystroke.

approaches.name: optimal: trie + per-query top-k
approaches.idea: Insert each sentence into a character trie; store the sentence's frequency at its terminal node (or a map at the node). Maintain a pointer to the trie node for the current prefix, advancing one edge per input(c). To answer, DFS the subtree under the current node collecting (freq, sentence) for all terminals, and take the top 3 with a heap or partial sort using the (freq desc, sentence asc) comparator. On a missing edge, the prefix has no matches and stays 'dead' until '#'.
approaches.time: O(p) to walk + O(m) to gather + O(m log k) to select

approaches.name: optimization: cache top-k at each trie node
approaches.idea: Store, at every node, a precomputed list of the top-k sentences passing through it. Retrieval becomes O(1) per keystroke. Updates on '#' cost O(L * k) to refresh top-k along the inserted path. Trades write cost and memory for very fast reads — the right call for read-heavy autocomplete.

follow_ups: Cache top-k at each node for O(1) retrieval — how do you update the cached lists on insert/frequency change without a full re-DFS?
Fuzzy / typo-tolerant autocomplete: return matches within edit distance 1 of the prefix (trie traversal with a bounded edit budget / DFA).
Personalized or recency-weighted ranking: blend global frequency with per-user history and time decay.
Scale to a huge corpus that doesn't fit on one machine: shard the trie by first characters, fan out queries, merge top-k from shards.
Memory reduction: compress to a radix/Patricia trie or a DAWG (shared suffixes); tradeoffs vs. update cost.
Weighted trie with a max-heap over children so retrieval explores high-frequency branches first and can stop early.
reference.reference_solution: Data model: TrieNode { children: map<char, TrieNode>, counts: map<sentence,int> } — storing counts at each node on the path lets retrieval read directly, or store frequency only at terminal nodes and DFS. State: root, a 'current' node pointer starting at root, and a 'prefix' string buffer. Build: for each (sentence,freq), insert(sentence, freq) walking/creating child nodes and setting terminal count += freq. input(c): if c == '#': insert(prefix, +1); prefix = ''; current = root; return []. else: prefix += c; if current is not null and c in current.children: current = current.children[c]; else current = null (dead prefix). Then retrieve: if current is null return []; collect all (count, sentence) terminals in current's subtree via DFS; select top 3 with a comparator that sorts by count descending then sentence ascending (a size-3 min-heap keyed by (count, reversed-lexicographic) works, or just sort the gathered list). Return the sentences. Optimization: keep at each node a cached hot list of its top-3; then input(c) just moves the pointer and reads current.top3 in O(1); on '#', walk the inserted path and update each node's cached top-3 given the changed count. The 'dead prefix' short-circuit (once current is null it stays null until '#') avoids re-searching after a miss.
pitfalls: Wrong tie-break: must be frequency DESC then sentence ASC (lexicographic); mixing these ranks incorrectly.
Rebuilding the prefix walk from the root on every keystroke instead of advancing a saved pointer.
Forgetting spaces are valid characters in the key.
On '#', not incrementing an existing sentence's count (treating a repeat as new) or not resetting the pointer to root.
Not short-circuiting a dead prefix, so you keep scanning after there's provably no match.
Collecting all matches and full-sorting when only top-3 is needed (use a bounded heap / partial selection).

interviewer_notes: This is a design-flavored coding problem; watch that the candidate nails the exact contract before coding — the '#' save-and-reset and the freq-desc-then-lexicographic tie-break are where sloppy candidates lose points, so let them state it and correct them only via the worked example if they get the tie-break backwards. The core structure should be a trie; if they propose scanning a hashmap each keystroke, accept it then ask 'what's the per-keystroke cost with 10^5 sentences?' to push them to the trie and to advancing a pointer rather than re-walking from root. The senior escalation is the retrieval-vs-precompute tradeoff: get them to first do per-query DFS+heap for top-k, then ask how they'd make retrieval O(1) (cache top-k at each node) and how to keep those caches updated on insert — that update story separates senior from staff. Further stretches: typo-tolerance (bounded edit distance over the trie) and sharding the trie across machines with top-k merge. Stay silent while they build the basic trie; nudge only on the tie-break or the dead-prefix short-circuit.
